title: Belavadös Night Sky
subtitle: A historical-style celestial analysis using Belavadös stars, moons, planets, constellation naming conventions, and Earth-facing sky time
document_type: Celestial lore reference • moons • wandering worlds • stars • constellations • sky-time conversion
naming_and_replacement_rules: The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.
The sky analysis keeps the historical-style latitude, precession, seasonality, and horizon logic, but is written as Belavadös sky lore rather than a modern archaeological report.

coordinate_system.summary: The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.

terms.meaning_in_this_document: Right Ascension, measured from 0h to 24h in hours, minutes, and seconds.
Declination, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator.
Astronomical Unit, used for planet distances.
Brightness as seen from the surface: lower is brighter.
Approximate maximum height above the horizon for an observer near 30° N latitude.

summary: Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.
formula_notes: 1. daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
time_conversion.player_facing_observing_log_format: Player-facing observing log format Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note. Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.

historical_style_sky_setting: The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise. The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and the eight named constellations would have served as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.

star_river.name: Star-River of Belavadös
star_river.description: The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions. From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

nebula_fields.name: Âhufej
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Foreground soot lanes (900 ly), dense emission nursery (1,380 ly), red-brown rear cloud (5,800 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Dense newborn stellar nursery with glowing hydrogen chambers. Rose tones arise from ionized hydrogen, gold from embedded young stars illuminating dust grains, while smoke-violet regions form where cooler molecular gas mingles with shadowed dust curtains. Texture resembles folded velvet mixed with branching smoke channels. Numerous protostars, Bok globules, and accretion knots are embedded throughout.

nebula_fields.name: Dus‘idu
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Silver strand foreground (1,100 ly), supernova shell (2,100 ly), violet mutation veil (6,200 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Extremely filamentary remnant structure. Cyan and jade hues indicate oxygen-rich shock fronts while white regions mark compressed gas where multiple shock waves intersect. Texture appears as torn silk, braided tendrils, and lace-like membranes. Contains expanding ejecta sheets, ionized oxygen filaments, sulfur traces, and high-energy particle fronts.

nebula_fields.name: Ềdizfu
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Foreground sparks (1,800 ly), storm sheet (4,200 ly), primary rift flower (5,600 ly), violet dust rear layer (7,900 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Vast petal-shaped dark nebula carved through a glowing emission field. Crimson and magenta petals surround blue-black voids where dense molecular dust blocks starlight. Texture resembles layered flower petals made of smoke and velvet. Contains cold molecular clouds, active collapse zones, dark filaments, and bright ionization ridges outlining the rift edges.

nebula_fields.name: Juçdimx
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Front ash layer (2,000 ly), reflective dust basin (3,400 ly), curse smoke (5,100 ly), under-road shadow (10,300 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: A highly reflective dust field illuminated by nearby blue stars. Silver and pearl regions arise from light scattering by fine silicate particles. Texture resembles finished frost, drifting fog banks, and layered mirror-glass sheets. Contains reflective silicate dust, carbonaceous smoke clouds, and fragmented molecular lanes.

nebula_fields.name: Jadd-Jisud
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Metal-blue shell (2,200 ly), green shell (4,800 ly), primary red-amber shell cluster (8,900 ly), lost-key echo layer (9,600 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Collection of overlapping planetary-nebula remnants. Amber and red shells arise from hydrogen and nitrogen emissions, while charcoal gaps reveal exhausted central cavities. Texture appears as stacked bubbles, fractured onion skins, and cracked glass spheres. Components include dying stellar cores, expanding gas shells, metallic ion clouds, and dusty ejecta rings.

nebula_fields.name: Horundar
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Tide mist (1,600 ly), reservoir core (1,900 ly), reef sheet (3,900 ly), blackwater wall (8,700 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Diffuse cloud filled with icy cometary material. White and ice-blue coloration results from starlight reflecting from frozen dust and microscopic ice crystals. Texture resembles sea fog, frost plumes, and submerged currents. Rich in volatile compounds, comet embryos, crystalline ice grains, and reflective dust sheets.

nebula_fields.name: Wougen
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Blue foreground haze (1,200 ly), star-forming core (2,850 ly), mirror sheet (3,600 ly), rose backwash (6,300 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: Massive molecular cloud actively producing stellar clusters. Green-gold regions arise from mixed oxygen and dust reflection, cream tones from warm embedded stars. Texture resembles billowing cream-colored thunderheads crossed by turquoise rivers. Components include molecular hydrogen reservoirs, stellar nurseries, evaporating gas pillars, and young cluster cavities.

nebula_fields.name: Ŝiowoei
nebula_fields.layer_structure: Silver foreground threads (2,000 ly), central spiral coil (4,200 ly), violet rear dust (7,900 ly)
nebula_fields.texture_and_components: A rotating spiral dust formation resembling a galactic whirlpool. Dark blue channels mark denser dust lanes while silver highlights indicate reflected starlight. Texture resembles braided ribbons, hurricane bands, and coiled smoke. Contains spiral molecular filaments, reflective silicates, and embedded star embryos tracing the coil arms.

worlds.intro: The Twelve Worlds of the Belavadös System The worlds orbit their star upon a relatively flat shared plane known as the Celestial Road. Belavadös itself remains the 1.00 AU reference world with a 330.15 Belavadös-day astronomical year; player-facing dates distribute that year evenly across the Earth calendar.

comets.name: Eiršu'neth Comet
comets.description: The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.

seasonal_sky_analysis.title: Winter evenings: The Minotaur Labyrinth ascends
seasonal_sky_analysis.summary: Winter evenings are dominated by The Minotaur Labyrinth of Anubaldir. Anubaldir Stone and Minotaur Eye mark the inner maze, while Goliath Horn and Firbolg Horn rise as paired tips above the bull-headed figure. Cyclopian Watch and Giff Burden form the lower gate and shoulder, making the shape read as both beast and maze. At 30° N, the Labyrinth's upper horn stars climb high while its lower gate remains mid-sky. Because the six stars sit between roughly RA 04h 51m and 06h 12m, the figure stays compact enough for a generator to draw a recognizable horned head rather than a scattered seasonal region.

seasonal_sky_analysis.title: Spring evenings: Mirror, Web, and Twin Drums
seasonal_sky_analysis.summary: Spring is the richest named-constellation season. The Luma Mirror of Nephthysra, The Silkborn Web of Thoryn-Rahek, and The Twin Drums of Ishtanora all become prominent. Their centers are deliberately separated in RA while their internal stars remain tightly grouped, allowing each figure to resolve as its own shape. This season is excellent for calendar work. The repeated appearance of three interlinked spring figures gives sky-watchers a stable sequence: the Web high in the north, the Mirror through the middle sky, and the Twin Drums balancing the equatorial zone.

seasonal_sky_analysis.title: Summer evenings: The Deep Gate and southern Star-River
seasonal_sky_analysis.summary: Summer brings the Sahuagin Deep Gate of Bastveig into the southern sky. Its upper lintel, twin pillars, and lower threshold span roughly RA 16h 01m to 17h 03m and Dec -18° to -46°, so the shape reads as a tall doorway rather than a diagonal scatter. The Star-River of Belavadös is most visually complex during this season. It would look bright, broken, and braided through the southern skyfields, then lift toward northern seasonal markers. The Deep Gate is deliberately horizon-sensitive, making it an oceanic and trench-associated marker.

seasonal_sky_analysis.title: Late summer and autumn: Crossroads Mask, Serpent, and Crown
seasonal_sky_analysis.summary: Late summer brings The Crossroads Mask of Freyseth low in the southern sky. The paired eye stars, hooked smile stars, and lower road-post star create a mask-like figure that is visible but vulnerable to haze, matching its lore of thresholds, temptation, and uncertain identity. As the cooling season advances, The Dragonborn Dominion of Valkhamesh and The Wechselkind Crown of Setrimir become defining figures. The Dominion forms a curving serpent at northern autumn declinations, while the Crown arcs around the 0h right-ascension seam without breaking the figure for a coordinate generator.

seasonal_sky_analysis.title: Circumpolar and horizon behavior
seasonal_sky_analysis.summary: At 30° N, the circumpolar threshold is approximately +60° declination. The named constellation stars remain below that threshold, so they rise and set rather than staying permanently visible. This preserves seasonal motion while still allowing high northern figures to climb impressively. The southern horizon limit is approximately -60° declination. The lowest named stars remain above that limit, so the Deep Gate and Crossroads Mask are visible from the assumed latitude, though dust, humidity, terrain, and haze can hide their faintest lower stars.

representative_night: A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the Minotaur Labyrinth and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N. When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.

practical_observing_guide: For winter navigation, begin with The Minotaur Labyrinth of Anubaldir: the two horn tips and maze-heart create the clearest cold-season figure.
For spring calendars, track the rising sequence of The Silkborn Web of Thoryn-Rahek, The Luma Mirror of Nephthysra, and The Twin Drums of Ishtanora.
For summer deep-sky watching, follow the Star-River of Belavadös through the southern skyfields toward The Sahuagin Deep Gate of Bastveig.
For late-summer horizon work, watch The Crossroads Mask of Freyseth; its lower road-post star is an excellent test of sky clarity.
For autumn ceremonial timing, use The Wechselkind Crown of Setrimir and The Dragonborn Dominion of Valkhamesh as high and mid-northern markers.

For lunar calendars, record both the broad phase of Chandratecu-Seleneš and the rapid position changes of Mictlindra-Nannara by using belSolarDayProgress, then display the result Earth-first with the local UTC label.
source_and_method_notes: The astronomical logic in this document uses standard sky-coordinate concepts: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, axial precession, and a 330.15-day Belavadös astronomical year distributed evenly across the Earth year for play. The values are intended for generators, lore notes, sky omens, transit boards, and table-facing observing logs.

No Earth star names are included. The document is intended as a lore-compatible sky reference for Belavadös and as a practical coordinate table for generators; the fixed stars are deliberately placed at remote background distances and several are faint enough to be only partially visible without unusually dark skies or magnification.
